teaser: The 2026 mega-listings priced trillion-dollar companies by selling a few per cent of them. What was sold, what it raised, and the founder's lesson.
core_idea: The headline valuations of the 2026 AI and space giants are set by selling small slices, as the share of companies sold at listing has fallen for decades; the money raised is large, revenue is real but profit mostly is not, multiples sit near the dot-com peak, and the founder's lesson is that control decides the size and terms of the slice.

quotes.text: The headline valuation is the last price paid for a slice, multiplied by everything.
A valuation is the price the market allows for the slice you choose to sell.

figures.caption: A small slice sets the price of the whole. At the IPO, 4.2% of SpaceX was sold at $135 a share, and the whole company was priced at $1.77tn. The valuations reported along the way were set the same way, by small transactions.
How much of each company was sold at its IPO, from the final prospectuses, with the median for all US IPOs since 1980 and for 2025 from Jay Ritter's statistics.
The biggest IPOs, base offering only, in September 2026 dollars; and, for three of them, the money raised as a share of the US stock market.
Valuation against a year of revenue: the dot-com peak, using trailing revenue, and the 2026 AI companies, using annualised run-rates.
